findings.title: Unauthenticated endpoint sends marketing email from your domain to any address

repro: curl -X POST https://www.lavacagc.com/api/leads/webhook -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{}'

evidence.impact: Anyone can send La Vaca-branded email to arbitrary recipients. Burns Resend quota, and sustained abuse degrades sending-domain reputation - which silently breaks deliverability for ALL mail including proposal links and receipts.

Remove it from PUBLIC_ROUTES and require INTERNAL_WEBHOOK_SECRET like /api/notify/*. If an external caller genuinely needs it, keep the secret and add a per-email rate limit.
remediation.risk: Low. Grep shows no first-party caller: the lead route imports createLeadFollowUpSequence directly.

findings.title: A raw POST can forge its own lead score and page you as a HOT lead

repro: LeadSubmitSchema ends in .passthrough() (src/app/api/leads/submit/route.ts:100), so unknown keys survive
sanitizeLeadForInsert accepts 'tier' (leadSanitize.ts:72), 'score' (:86) and 'scoring_reasons' (:88) as writable columns
route.ts:445 'if (!finalLeadData.score)' skips scoreLead entirely when the caller supplied one
evidence.expected: Lead score and tier are computed server-side from the lead's own content and are not client-writable
evidence.actual: A body containing {"score":100,"tier":"hot"} is stored verbatim and short-circuits scoring; the Telegram alert then renders 'New HOT Lead' / 'Score: 100/100'
evidence.impact: The prioritisation signal the owner acts on can be forged by anyone. Also poisons every downstream report that groups by tier, and there is no range check - negative or absurd scores store fine.

findings.rootCause: Trust boundary: .passthrough() lets caller-controlled keys reach the sanitizer, and the scoring step treats a caller-supplied score as authoritative.

remediation.approach: Strip server-owned columns from the request before sanitising, and always score server-side. Do not rely on the schema alone - the sanitizer is the chokepoint.
alsoApplyTo: any future server-computed column added to leadSanitize's TEXT_COLUMNS/INTEGER_COLUMNS
remediation.risk: Low. No form sends these fields today.

acceptanceCriteria.statement: A submit carrying score:100/tier:hot stores the server-computed score, not 100
A normal submission still gets a computed score and tier

verify.expect: score is a number 0-100 and tier in hot|warm|cold

acceptanceCriteria.statement: No server-owned column is writable through the public submit path

verify.expect: every SERVER_OWNED key is stripped before sanitise

findings.title: Rejected submissions alert you - so the rate limit buys an attacker 10 messages a minute

repro: checkRateLimit runs at route.ts:348, BEFORE the validation checks at :362 (recaptcha) and :375 (contact required)
Each of those failure paths calls reportFailure (:363, :376, :424) which fires 1 Telegram + 1 Resend (formErrorAlert.ts:83,124)
One junk key in an otherwise valid body triggers the sanitize warning alert at :495 - another Telegram + Resend
evidence.expected: A rejected request is cheap; alerting is reserved for failures the owner can act on
evidence.actual: 5 deliberately-invalid requests per minute per IP produce ~10 owner notifications per minute per IP
evidence.impact: An attacker can flood the owner's phone and inbox, and burn Resend quota, at 5 requests a minute - low enough to look like normal traffic. The consent route already solved this exact problem (consent/log/route.ts:48-50 deliberately does not alert on 429/400).

findings.rootCause: Validation failures are treated as system faults worth alerting on, and the alert sits inside the rate-limited path rather than behind its own budget.

remediation.approach: Do not alert on client-fault rejections (400/429). Alert only on server faults (5xx, DB write failures), and put a separate low ceiling on alerting itself.
remediation.risk: Low, but note the trade-off: genuine misconfiguration that causes mass 400s becomes quieter, so keep a daily digest.

acceptanceCriteria.statement: 20 invalid submissions produce zero owner alerts
A genuine server-side failure still alerts once
No public route fires an owner alert on a 4xx it generated itself

findings.title: Server-side database role has no statement timeout - one bad query can hold a connection for two minutes

repro: select rolname, rolconfig from pg_roles where rolname in ('anon','authenticated','service_role')
evidence.expected: Every role has a statement timeout short enough that a runaway query cannot exhaust the connection pool
evidence.actual: anon = 3s, authenticated = 8s, service_role = (none) -> falls back to the database default of 120s
evidence.impact: Every server-side query in this app runs as service_role (SUPABASE_SECRET_KEY). A single pathological query holds a pooled connection for two minutes; a handful exhausts the pool and takes the whole site down. This is the limit that protects the database from bugs nobody predicted, and it is the one that is missing.

findings.rootCause: service_role was never given a rolconfig statement_timeout, so it inherits the 120s database default.

remediation.approach: Set a statement timeout on service_role. 15s is generous for every query this app legitimately makes (the slowest measured route is far below it) while bounding the damage of a runaway one.
remediation.risk: Medium - a cron doing a genuinely long job would now be cut off. Audit the crons first; raise per-transaction where needed.

limitProposed.name: service_role statement_timeout
limitProposed.justification: Well above every measured query; far below the 120s that lets one query monopolise a connection.

acceptanceCriteria.statement: service_role can no longer run a query longer than the timeout

verify.sql: select rolconfig from pg_roles where rolname='service_role'

acceptanceCriteria.statement: Every cron route still completes inside the timeout
No role is left without a statement timeout

verify.sql: select rolname from pg_roles where rolname in ('anon','authenticated','service_role','authenticator') and (rolconfig is null or not (array_to_string(rolconfig,',') like '%statement_timeout%'))

findings.title: Capability tokens and customer PII are recorded by third-party analytics

repro: src/app/layout.tsx:108-128 loads Microsoft Clarity (session recording) and Meta Pixel on EVERY page, gated only on hostname and GPC - no path exclusion
src/components/Analytics.tsx:21 excludes only /admin, /vaca-mgmt and /auth from GA

evidence.impact: The token IS the credential: anyone with access to the Clarity account (or a breach of it) can replay the session and reuse a live token. findings.rootCause: Analytics is mounted globally in the root layout with an exclusion list that predates the token-authenticated surfaces.

findings.title: Rate limiter fails open, so every limit disappears exactly when the database is struggling

repro: rateLimit.ts:136 missing key/URL -> {allowed:true}
rateLimit.ts:151 any query error -> {allowed:true}
rateLimit.ts:194 any exception -> {allowed:true}
evidence.expected: A limiter that cannot check its budget makes a deliberate, observable decision
evidence.actual: It silently allows, with only a console.error
evidence.impact: Every endpoint whose sole protection is a rate limit becomes unprotected during a database incident. It is also a feedback loop: load slows the DB, the limiter's own query errors, the limiter opens, and the load is admitted at full rate. Compounds CM-03 (alert flooding) and CM-08 (ungated referrals).

findings.rootCause: Availability was chosen over protection, silently and without an alarm.

remediation.approach: Keep failing open for genuine outages - refusing real customers is worse - but make it loud and bounded: count the failures, alert once per window, and fail CLOSED for the endpoints whose abuse is expensive (anything that sends email or spends money).
remediation.risk: Medium - failing closed can reject legitimate traffic during an outage, which is why only the spend paths get it.

acceptanceCriteria.statement: With the limiter's backing store erroring, a spend-path request is refused
With the store healthy, traffic under the limit still passes
Every limiter fail-open path emits a degraded signal

findings.title: Member release email silently drops everyone past the thousandth recipient

repro: releases/send/route.ts:158-160 reads homeowners?status=eq.active with NO limit= clause
RECIPIENT_CAP = 1000 (:40); recipients = homeowners.slice(0, 1000) (:162)
truncated = homeowners.length - recipients.length (:163)
evidence.expected: If more members exist than can be mailed in one run, the admin is told
evidence.actual: PostgREST applies its own default row ceiling to an uncapped request, so homeowners.length can never exceed the cap the code slices at. truncated is therefore structurally always 0.
evidence.impact: Past the ceiling, members silently never receive the release and the UI reports zero truncation. Latent today (4 active members) and certain at scale. The guard the author wrote cannot fire.
evidence.invariantBroken: A truncation counter must be computed from a total the caller controls, never from a page the server sized.

findings.rootCause: The row cap is implicit (PostgREST's default) rather than explicit, so the code cannot distinguish 'exactly 1000' from 'at least 1000'.

remediation.approach: Ask for one more row than the cap so truncation is detectable, or read an exact count. Then either mail in batches or report honestly.
alsoApplyTo: every uncapped read listed in chaos/recon-queries.md - the same implicit-ceiling trap

acceptanceCriteria.statement: With more active members than the cap, truncated is greater than zero
With fewer members than the cap, all are mailed and truncated is 0
No query relies on the server's implicit row ceiling: every read that feeds a count or a cap sets limit= explicitly

findings.title: Server accepts data every browser form rejects, including unvalidated email

repro: email: optStr(320) with NO format check (route.ts:72) while all six forms enforce z.string().email() or a regex
phone optStr(60), zip optStr(20), first/last name optStr(200), city optStr(200) - no server regex against client rules at ContactForm.tsx:44,49,58 and EstimateForm.tsx:52,67,76,80
/api/home-care/subscribe already does it right: z.string().email().max(320)
evidence.expected: The server is at least as strict as the browser, because the browser is not a security control
evidence.actual: The client is stricter on email format, phone shape, ZIP shape, name charset and length caps

The email case is the worst: garbage passes the schema, the lead row is created, and then createLeadFollowUpSequence refuses to send (leadFollowUp.ts:122) - so the customer gets no acknowledgement and the only trace is a log line. That is silent lead damage, the failure class this project already has history with.

findings.rootCause: The submit schema was written to be maximally forgiving (optStr truncates rather than rejects) so a lead is never lost, and format checking was never added back at the layer that could reject safely.

remediation.approach: Keep the forgiving posture for optional fields, but validate the two that decide whether the lead is contactable at all. Reject an unparseable email outright rather than storing a lead that can never be answered.
remediation.risk: Medium - tightening a lead intake path can reject real submissions. Ship behind a log-only mode first: record what WOULD have been rejected for a week before enforcing.

findings.title: An oversized number in a submission destroys the lead with a 500

repro: square_footage and visit_count are absent from LeadSubmitSchema, so they ride .passthrough() uncapped
leadSanitize.ts:131 Math.trunc accepts 9e99 because Number.isFinite(9e99) is true

findings.title: Reads that grow with the business have no row cap

repro: ConversionDashboard.tsx:110 reads leads with no .limit()
admin/dashboard/route.ts:38 reads a 30-day email_log slice with no cap, plus three exact counts
admin/follow-ups/route.ts:39 selects * from follow_up_queue where each row carries full rendered email HTML
portfolio/page.tsx:92 and ProjectGallery.tsx:121 issue one project_images query per project
evidence.expected: Query count stays flat as row count grows, and every read of a growing table states its ceiling
evidence.actual: Roughly 45 reads have no explicit cap and silently inherit the server's ceiling; several loops issue one query per row
evidence.impact: LATENT. Today the largest table is ~12k rows and the rest are in the hundreds, so nothing is slow and no load test would show anything. After launch these become slow pages, truncated dashboards that silently under-report, and - combined with CM-04's missing statement timeout - a route that can hold connections long enough to affect the whole site.

findings.rootCause: PostgREST returns a bounded page by default, so an uncapped read looks correct in every test written against small data.

remediation.approach: Treat it as one class, not 45 bugs. Add an explicit cap to every read of a growing table, make the cap visible in the response so truncation is never silent, and add a lint that fails the build on a new uncapped read.
alsoApplyTo: every row in the uncapped-reads table in chaos/recon-queries.md
remediation.risk: Low per site, but there are many; do the growing tables first (leads, email_log, follow_up_queue, homeowners, seo_metrics).

acceptanceCriteria.statement: Query count for each instrumented route does not grow as rows grow
Every list view still shows its data at small scale
A newly added uncapped read of a growing table fails the build
A truncated list reports truncation rather than showing a silently short list

attemptLog: Investigated all 38 baselined violations rather than capping them blindly. 33 were FALSE POSITIVES of the checker itself, in four classes: (a) limit= present in a concatenated second template chunk the regex never read, (b) reads bounded by an equality filter on a parent id/email, (c) filters held in a local variable and interpolated, (d) helpers returning a query BUILDER for the caller to finish. The checker was fixed for each; it also reported wrong line numbers because it stripped comments before counting lines.

The 5 real ones were fixed by category: a counting read now asks for only as many rows as the threshold it tests; two cron work queues became bounded batches that REPORT their remainder rather than dropping it silently; two narrow reads got explicit caps.
